summary: Carney and Xi widen their trade deal in Shenzhen, with China dropping tariffs on Canadian pork and shrimp, while inflation held at 3.1% in October as gas and groceries rose.
body: Prime Minister Mark Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday, their second meeting this year.[^1] China will remove its 25% tariff on Canadian frozen pork and cold-water shrimp, plus some other seafood, worth about $400 million a year in exports, Carney's office says. China will also open its market to Canadian fava beans, chickpeas and lentils.[^1] In return, Canada will let 32 more kinds of Chinese steel and aluminum in without extra duties where Canadian supply falls short. Canola oil still faces a Chinese duty.[^1] Carney told Xi the two countries can "work together more broadly, pragmatically", while saying sensitive areas like critical minerals and AI stay off limits.[^1]

Not everyone likes the direction. Trump trade adviser Peter Navarro accused Carney on X of trying to play China off against the US.[^2] Carney says any Chinese car plant would have to bring real jobs; about 16,200 Chinese EVs have entered Canada since March under this year's quota.[^1] Carney also said he would raise foreign interference; China denies it interferes.[^2]

At home, Statistics Canada said inflation held at 3.1% in October, slightly below the 3.2% economists expected.[^3][^4] Gas was up 30.9% from a year ago, partly because prices were low last October, and grocery prices rose 2.0%, while phone plans got cheaper.[^3] Clothing jumped 3.4% in one month, the biggest rise since 2019, which StatCan links to higher shipping costs.[^3] Without energy, inflation was 2.0%. The Bank of Canada decides on rates again on Dec. 9.[^3][^5]
differences: Ottawa presents the deal as practical trade with "clear guardrails"; Trump adviser Peter Navarro calls it an attempt to play China off the US, and rights activists were alarmed by Xi's call to set differences aside.[^1][^2]
